Two high-ranking defectors — a former intelligence officer and a commander in Iran's elite special forces — went on the record. Using burner phones, encrypted apps and code words, DW's investigative unit spent months verifying their identities and the documents, photos and footage they shared.

items.title: The Dolomites - Summer in the Italian Alps | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>From rugged peaks to gentle valleys, Italy's Dolomites are idyllic. In this film, nature lovers show us their mountain world and share fascinating stories about life between tradition and modernity.

In the Dolomites, Italy's "dolce vita" culture meets Alpine tradition — the perfect combination for anyone who wants spectacular natural scenery coupled with a diverse culinary scene. Beyond better-known tourist destinations like Seiser Alm, the Tre Cime di Lavaredo and the Rosengarten, there is much to discover in the Dolomites — or "pale mountains". In the Friulian Dolomites Nature Park, a team of biologists, veterinarians and animal rangers saves the life of an ibex by performing emergency surgery on a crooked horn. 

South of Bolzano, a photographer captures the portraits of elderly mountain farmers and alpinists from remote valleys as part of a UNESCO project — using camera technology that's over a century old. A young shepherd couple spends their summer on a secluded high pasture near the Valles Pass, relishing their modest Alpine lifestyle. An entrepreneur from Trento, a city on the Adige River, makes speaker cabinets from the wood of trees felled by a hurricane, while investing in local reforestation. And in Val Gardena, on one of the oldest farms in the Alps, a family offers guests a menu of traditional Ladin food — the regional cuisine — made with ingredients they grow themselves.

items.title: Mao Zedong and the founding of the People's Republic of China (2/3) | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>From peasants' son to revolutionary leader — Mao Zedong laid the foundation for modern China. This three-part documentary offers an in-depth look at one of the most influential figures of the 20th century. *Part 3 coming soon!*

Part 1: https://youtu.be/dP8dX4Pyzd0
Part 2: https://youtu.be/kml_5jNV0j8
Part 3: Available from 17 October 2026

The legacy of the "founding father" of the People's Republic of China remains deeply controversial. Revered in Europe as a revolutionary icon in the late 1960s, Mao led China to the brink of disaster and ultimately clung to power with a regime of terror. Yet today's leaders in Beijing continue to draw on the cult of Mao. China is now a global power, a transformation that would be difficult to imagine without Mao Zedong.

When Mao Zedong was born in 1893, nothing hinted at his meteoric rise to power. The son of a farming family, he grew up during a period of political instability and profound social upheaval. The 1911 Revolution, which marked the beginning of the end of imperial rule, awakened his mind to politics. At first, Mao had no clear political program. But the Russian Revolution of 1917 introduced him to Marxist ideas, and he soon became a co-founder of the Communist Party of China.

Mao rose steadily through the party ranks as conflict with the nationalist Kuomintang party intensified into a bloody civil war. The devastating retreat that became known as the "Long March" went down in history to become the foundation of the cult of Mao. After World War II, the struggle for power in China continued until Mao and his forces finally reached Beijing.

This three-part series traces Mao Zedong's journey from peasants' son to revolutionary and architect of modern China — from his rural childhood to the founding of the People's Republic to the devastating impact of the Cultural Revolution in the 1960s, which claimed millions of lives.

Archival footage, as well as interviews with historians and eyewitnesses, tell the story of the man who changed China forever.

items.title: Skin: Multitalented and underappreciated | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Our skin connects us to the world while also providing us with a boundary and a layer of protection. It's a biotope, an object of desire, and it allows us to smell the way we do. How can we keep our skin healthy, and heal it when it's unwell?

On average, the skin is around two square meters in area and weighs between five and ten kilograms. For a long time, it was viewed primarily as a covering. But this multitalented organ is much more than that. It provides us with one of our senses, it can draw oxygen directly from the air, and it can even perceive sound waves and odor molecules.

The skin is also a status symbol, with smooth, wrinkle-free skin symbolizing youth, beauty and success. Countless experts offer advice, including recommending anti-aging products containing acids, bases, enzymes, vitamins, or proteins. But only a few cosmetics are truly worth it, says dermatologist Professor Claudia Borelli of the University Hospital in Tübingen, Germany. The same goes for the advice of many skincare influencers, who often promote their own interests on social media. So is it better to think twice before rushing to get cosmetic treatments?

Over the past five years, procedures using Botox and hyaluronic acid have more than doubled. Borelli warns that poorly administered fillers can cause problems for years to come. Nevertheless, the clients of cosmetic doctors are getting younger and younger. Gaming streamer Jasmin Gnu had lip fillers in her early 20s — she now regrets that decision. She tells her fans that they don't have to chase the unattainable aesthetic ideals sold to them by the beauty filters used on social media.

Meanwhile, the skin can also be seen as a window into the soul. Stress can make the skin sick, says psychodermatologist Professor Uwe Gieler. About a quarter of Germans suffer from skin conditions such as atopic dermatitis, psoriasis, acne, or allergies. With the help of an anti-inflammatory diet, new medications and therapy, there's a good chance of healing unhealthy skin.

DESCRIPTION
Garrison Hinson-Hasty, author of “Systems Programming with Zig” and a contributor to the Zig compiler, joins Trevor Berrange Sanchez to explain why he wrote a book on a pre-1.0 language that breaks frequently (he's currently updating the last seven chapters for Zig 0.16). His answer: the language's slow march toward 1.0 is a feature, and learning it now teaches you why its decisions stick. The conversation's core thesis is that Zig is countercultural: instead of stacking new abstractions on old ones, it reuses well-tested ideas and "never adds too much”. "Simple", in the Zig community's sense, means simple relative to what the machine is doing, with integer and pointer types that map closely to how you'd think about data in assembly. Chapter 6's CHIP-8 interpreter shows this: a few integers, some buffers, and elegant results. The same philosophy explains Zig's missing string type. Strings are just byte sequences with a length, and the language leaves encoding choices to you. Garrison notes that Rust, by contrast, now has to maintain its many string types forever.

Two practical takeaways for working engineers. First, allocators: because Zig encourages flat, data-oriented design, the book barely needs dynamic allocation, and when it does, allocators let you reason about memory for a whole phase of a program (say, a compiler's parser) as one unit rather than tracking the lifetime of every AST node. Second, C interop: you can use a C header directly, keep defer for cleanup instead of goto, and write small Zig wrappers around awkward C error-return conventions. The chapter on graphics and OpenGL, meanwhile, is really about a transferable systems skill: working out what an unfamiliar, committee-designed API wants from you when no tutorial exists.

Salamatty Kazakhstan was launched by the government to improve medical care in the country's sparsely populated regions. Some communities are hundreds of kilometers from the nearest hospital or clinic. The train's timetable is shared online.

In addition to medical staff, the train crew includes kitchen staff, stewards, and technicians. On its journey of around 20,000 kilometers, the train stops in numerous villages and small towns in the Kazakh countryside. The film follows this unique social project, showing doctors and support staff as they form close bonds during the eight-month journey: working, eating and living together. Patients come to the clinic with physical ailments, but they also share their everyday worries.

The film offers a rare glimpse into this oil-rich Central Asian country. It gives viewers a sense of the respect and dedication at the heart of these special encounters between two very different worlds.
